discovery: Harvesting triplet excitons for efficient organic light emission: electrophosphorescence and thermally activated delayed fluorescence

nominees.name: Stephen R. Forrest
nominees.affiliation: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA

nominees.name: Mark E. Thompson
nominees.affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA

subfield: Condensed matter physics: organic semiconductors and optoelectronics
motivation: Spin statistics dictate that electrical injection into molecular semiconductors forms three triplet excitons for every singlet, and triplets are normally dark. This set a fundamental 25% ceiling on the efficiency of organic light-emitting diodes. Forrest and Thompson showed in 1998 that heavy-metal complexes with strong spin-orbit coupling make triplets emissive, and electrophosphorescence reached close to 100% internal quantum efficiency. Adachi, who contributed to that early work, later showed that molecules designed with a very small singlet-triplet exchange splitting return triplets to the singlet state thermally (TADF). This gave a route to full exciton harvesting without precious metals. Together these advances turned a clear insight into exciton spin physics into the working basis of OLED displays, which billions of people now use. They also changed how the whole field thinks about controlling spin in molecular materials.
